body.text: The steady deterioration in India-US relations, the near-simultaneous warming of ties between India and China, and the emerging tactical rapprochement between Washington and Beijing are mutually reinforcing dynamics. The reduced strategic value of India in US grand strategy, paired with Washington’s willingness to manage its relations with China directly, is reassuring for Beijing, which was anxious about a US-led encirclement, making it more receptive to India’s overtures. This shift, however, is troubling for India, which must keep all policy options open, including stabilising its relationship with China, to avoid strategic obsolescence amid an evolving superpower bargain. Paradoxically, the US remains a crucial diplomatic, security, economic and technological partner for India, even as New Delhi continues to view Beijing with deep strategic mistrust.

Historically, bilateral dynamics within this triad have cast long shadows over the broader triangle, with each power viewing the other two through the prism of its relations with the third. These pushes and pulls closely mirror the interactions among the Vijigishu (aspirant state), the Madhyama (the middle or intermediate king), and the Udasina (the neutral king) in Kautilya’s Rajamandala (circle of states) theory of the interstate realm. Lessons from this ancient Indian treatise on statecraft offer insights into the strategic intentions of these geographically distinct, asymmetric powers.

Kautilya’s Rajamandala theory is a rigorously conceptualised model of interstate conduct in which different categories of states, defined by their geographical location, relative strength and intentions, vie to increase their comprehensive national power. It envisages the international theatre as it is today: one where rules-based orders are an anomaly rather than the norm. Applied to the present shift in world order, the theory offers a compelling template to decode the US-India-China dynamics.

If India is modelled as the Vijigishu (the ambitious, aspirational state seeking to preserve its strategic autonomy and expand its influence), China fits the role of a quintessential Madhyama (the intermediate power). Positioned along the immediate borders of both the Vijigishu and its Ari (the continuous adversary, Pakistan), the Madhyama possesses the raw power to assist or coerce either state depending on whether the two act in unison or remain divided.

The US is the clear Udasina situated outside the primary continental sphere of the Vijigishu, Ari and Madhyama; stronger than their constituents; capable of helping the enemy, the conqueror and the middle king when they are united or disunited and of suppressing them when they are disunited. While its geographical detachment affords the luxury of neutrality, its stakes in the Indo-Pacific compel it to take sides, sow dissension and offer capabilities to prevent the rise of a hegemon. How these three powers conduct themselves with one another reveals these ancient mechanics in real time.

For more than two decades, India has attempted to cultivate the Udasina (US) as its Mitra (ally). Despite its inherent caution about partnering with a superior power and risking the erosion of its decision-making autonomy, New Delhi's apprehensions were eased by strong strategic convergence (namely, the China ‘glue’) and domestic capacity that lagged behind its rising global aspirations. That US backing could add to India’s weight in the international system and single-handedly make India a new great power was a credible possibility, acknowledged even by Chinese strategic analysts. However, the warmth in the bilateral relationship began to fade as Washington confronted the limits of its expectations, realising it had placed a bad bet on India if it had anticipated that India would formally join an anti-China military camp.

The multi-sectoral assistance India received from Washington over the years was never “dana” (the virtue of selfless charity). Even when viewed through the Kautilyan framework of Upayas (Sama [conciliation], Dana [gift-giving], Bheda [sowing dissension], Danda [use of force]), US dana was a political method designed to enlist India as a partner in service of Washington’s strategic interests. Offers to supply advanced military technology, co-produce and co-develop military equipment, strengthen India’s maritime and naval capacity, and extend full support to India in the event of another border crisis are helpful and compatible with US interests. These overtures were driven not by altruism but by a clear strategic objective—balancing China, Washington’s primary adversary, in the Indo-Pacific.

From a Kautilyan perspective, US disenchantment is predictable. In an asymmetric alliance, the stronger partner supports the weaker one only so long as their strategic trajectories are aligned. Kautilya prescribes that the superior power should not allow its partner to become either too weak or too powerful, keeping it strong enough to resist the primary enemy but not so strong as to assert its strategic upmanship. This logic echoes US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau’s 2026 statement that the US will not repeat the “China mistake” with India.

Nevertheless, the China glue remains sticky enough to sustain the relationship in the longer term. As with cooperation in other mutually beneficial sectors, pragmatism will prevail over tactical anxieties. US investment in Pakistan or Bangladesh as alternative regional counterweights to China remains unpersuasive. As long as the Udasina remains broadly favourable to the Vijigishu’s wider network in the Rajamandala, the Vijigishu should be favourable to the Udasina.

The relationship between India and China resonates with Kautilya’s dynamic between the Vijigishu and the Madhyama. Positioned along India’s immediate borders and having the power to influence both India and its Ari (Pakistan), China acts as a classical Madhyama. In the Kautilyan scheme, the Vijigishu remains favourably inclined towards the Madhyama only if the latter respects his security sphere. If the Madhyama coerces the Vijigishu’s allies, Kautilya prescribes counteractive measures: inciting regional allies, dividing the Madhyama from its partners, and rousing the allies of the ally. If the Madhyama seeks to seize the neutral king (Udasina), the Vijigishu should aid the Madhyama, thinking, “Let him be separated from the neutral.”

The ancient logic illuminates the changing dynamics between China and India. Following the 2020 Galwan Valley clash and the breakdown of 1990s border protocols, China solidified its position as India’s primary security challenge. Much of China’s hostility during this period was attributable to India’s deepening ties with the US—marked by India’s Major Defence Partner status, foundational agreements (the Logistics Exchange Memorandum of Agreement [LEMOA], the Communications Compatibility and Security Agreement [COMCASA] and the Basic Exchange and Cooperation Agreement [BECA]), the revival of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) and the India-US 2+2 dialogues. Beijing perceived this as a serious threat, with New Delhi serving as Washington’s frontline balancer.

The structural mechanics of the triangle have shifted once again. Recent friction in India-US ties, combined with Beijing’s assessment that US “strategic altruism” has reached its limits because of India’s firm strategic autonomy, has largely defused China’s primary fear of a US-led encirclement.

For New Delhi, navigating these triadic dynamics requires a fine balancing act. Structural friction between India and China benefits the US; friction between India and the US benefits China; and competition between the US and China has historically strengthened India’s strategic leverage. As India's External Affairs Minister (EAM) cautioned on Sino-Indian friction, “third parties will take advantage”—an observation that stems from Kautilya’s warnings on triadic vulnerability.

With the US becoming more transactional and unpredictable and the spectre of a US-China bargain looming, India’s strategic flexibility rests on managing its continental neighbour on its own terms. Beyond geopolitical prudence, New Delhi’s recent tactical stabilisation with Beijing reflects a stark structural reality: deep economic interdependence and a reliance on Chinese supply chains to power domestic industrialisation.

Navigating the choice between the Madhyama (China) and the Udasina (US) is complicated by a modern reality that ancient texts did not fully anticipate: prevailing US transactionalism, which frequently veers from rational-actor behaviour. Compounding this is India’s unique structural position in its Rajamandala—marked by substantial yet growing national power—which precludes both foolhardy valour and spineless submission in addressing the China challenge.

Kautilya prescribes, “Between the middle and neutral kings, the conqueror shall lean towards that king who is liked by his circle of kings.” Furthermore, if the Udasina opposes the Madhyama, the Vijigishu should prefer the power that helps it outmanoeuvre the primary adversary (Ari), supports its allies, or provides direct military capabilities. Yet Kautilya allows a marginal preference for the Madhyama because of its geographical contiguity. He also envisages scenarios in which the interests of the Madhyama and the Udasina converge, and dictates that the Vijigishu should make peace with the Madhyama when doing so serves its own ends while placating the intermediate power. In contemporary terms, this offers Beijing a crucial window to recognise New Delhi’s strategic value beyond the lens of US competition.

In the longer run, India’s structural interests align more closely with the US than with China. India’s rise, at whatever pace, inevitably rouses a Chinese state intent on maintaining regional hegemony. Even Washington may see China’s reassurance that cooperation can avoid the “Thucydides Trap” as a tactical manoeuvre to manage superpower friction, one that would ultimately give way to great-power rivalry. For New Delhi, strategic leverage is at its maximum when Washington and Beijing remain locked in a sustained, controlled strategic competition: strong enough to perpetuate hostility, but tempered enough to avoid direct military confrontation.

Ultimately, Kautilyan statecraft offers no substitute for internal balancing. In the long run, investments in India’s Janapada—its territory, population and domestic capacity—will yield decisive results. External alignments and triadic diplomacy remain tactical buffers. Modern geopolitics, however, affords India little time, while also precluding any attempt to augment its power in isolation.

As economic interdependencies are increasingly weaponised for strategic leverage, building domestic capacity has become an urgent race against time. In the near term, New Delhi must prioritise critical inputs from both sides of the triangle to accelerate its internal rise: cutting-edge technology, defence co-production and advanced capital from Washington; and stable access to active pharmaceutical ingredients and manufacturing inputs essential to domestic industrialisation from Beijing. To broaden its strategic options and hedge against superpower deal-making, India must also deepen ties with like-minded middle powers, including Japan, Australia and France, as well as other European partners.

By building its comprehensive national power while navigating triadic dynamics on a case-by-case basis, India can advance its foundational ambition as a Vijigishu and preserve its strategic autonomy in an anarchic world.
